articles.title: New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator , in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.
SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero . That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.
With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.
Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.
The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

articles.title: From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.
Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.
“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.
Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.
Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March .

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.
Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.
“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.
Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet . Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.
The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development , but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.
“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.
Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025 , grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.
Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.
“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

articles.title: Ballard Starter Line
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting Sound Transit made it clear that they do not want to make any major changes to the BLE plans to avoid starting all over with the EIS process. They did consider at some point starting with a connection between Ballard and Westlake and delay or even skip the second downtown tunnel (DSTT2). But that would require a separate operations and maintenance facility (OMF) at Interbay or connecting to the existing downtown tunnel (DSTT1). The tunnel is old and surrounding soil is unstable and therefore they concluded this would be very risky and costly. Tom Terrific however suggested a single-track maintenance tunnel connection which would connect at the end of the current tunnel by the Convention Center.

While any major design change (such as an elevated line) may jeopardize the current EIS process, implementing a project in phases is common and accepted. Not spending $8b on a second downtown tunnel at this point would allow Sound Transit to connect Ballard much earlier (in particular if paired with other measures such as automating the line or a ship canal gondola ). With all the downtown complexities it would also reduce a lot of risks. And as almost half of the tunnel is covered by funds collected in Pierce and Snohomish County and the Eastside, it may even allow Sound Transit to finish the spine earlier, a goal the Board keeps reiterating.

Sound Transit has also stated that the Ballard line is necessary to connect to the Tacoma line as an Everett to Tacoma line would get too long for operators, but they could turn Tacoma trains around at Northgate or just change operators halfway.

Sound Transit studied alternatives for a second tunnel. Either the line could connect to the existing tunnel (interlining) by tapping into the existing tunnel at Pine St and 3rd or operate as a separate line with a separate OMF at Interbay. They determined that both options would not be any cheaper than proceeding with a second tunnel. I tend to agree with the risks involved with tapping the existing tunnel for interlining. However, Tom’s suggestion for a single track to connect a Ballard line with the existing tunnel should warrant further research. To reduce operational impact, such track could be used during off-hours. It would allow maintaining trains at the SODO OMF instead of having to build a separate OMF.

Before the original tunnel was extended to Capitol Hill with a slight curve to the south, it used to have a track extending straight east of the Westlake station for trains to turn around. It might be possible to extend that tunnel portion and add a north turn. You may need to use the I-5 Express Lane exit to build such track. That track could then connect with the Ballard line roughly at the Denny station. It would be fairly long but for a maintenance track that should not matter as much.

Adding such a maintenance tunnel would be expensive, but not nearly as much as building a second tunnel or a separate Interbay OMF. I hope it would allow Sound Transit to serve Ballard well before 2042.

articles.title: The Urbanist is Hiring an Operations Strategist
articles.author: Diego Batres
paras: The Urbanist is seeking a term-limited Operations Strategist to help strengthen our organizational systems and infrastructure as we continue to grow.

This temporary, project-based role will focus on building and improving our operations policies and procedures including financial management, information systems, donor and membership infrastructure, and organizational compliance. The Operations Strategist will work closely with our Board of Directors to build sustainable systems and lay the groundwork for a permanent Operations Manager position.
We are open to either a term-limited employee or an independent consultant for this role, with a budget of up to $70,000. Work is expected to begin in January 2027 and conclude by July 31, 2027.
Read the full job description and application instructions at www.theurbanist.org/jobs .

The Urbanist is committed to hiring and advancing personnel from traditionally underrepresented communities with an explicit regard to Black people, Indigenous people, people of color, immigrants, LGBTQIA people, and disabled people.

articles.title: 'The Forge District': Kirkland Gives NE 85th Station Area a Rebrand
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The City of Kirkland is hoping a new name for the area around a forthcoming bus rapid transit station can aid in revitalization efforts, after years of lackluster development activity there. Last week, the Kirkland City Council picked "The Forge District" as its preferred moniker for the area after considering several other alternatives for a rebrand that is intended to foster a "distinct identity" and punch up marketing for potential developers.

NE 85th Street Station, situated in the median of I-405, will see double-decker express bus service starting in 2029 as part of the Sound Transit S2 line , and existing ST Express buses will stop at the interchange as soon as next year. But the development spark that city leaders have been hoping to see in the immediate area has not yet caught fire, despite a 2023 rezone that provided significant development capacity.

About a mile from the heart of Kirkland's charming downtown, the 710-acre station area stands at the confluence of several other neighborhoods including Rose Hill, Everest, and Norkirk. Though the vision is a "thriving, new walkable district with high tech and family wage jobs, plentiful affordable housing, sustainable buildings, park amenities, and commercial and retail services linked by transit," the area remains dominated by car dealerships, drive-through businesses today, and the freeway looming overhead.

Following the selection of a name, a visual branding scheme will follow, "to create collateral to support retention and recruitment of businesses, property owners, developers, and investors," according to a staff report provided to councilmembers.

"When we talk about the naming for NE 85th, it's not just for us as current community members or business owners, but it is also looking at those who will be coming here in the future," Jen Davis Hayes, Kirkland's Economic Development Manager, said ahead of the final naming vote.

Why the Forge? "Heat, energy," noted a presentation created by the consultant company Watson Creative. "Complimentary juxtaposition to softer Rose Hill, Norkirk, Juanita, Houghton, Totem Lake, Bridle Trails."
"Scales well: Forge Building, Forge Station, Forge Park."

The Forge District also references the steel foundry built by the city's namesake, Peter Kirk, in 1890. That steel mill "never produced a single ingot," according to the Kirkland Heritage Society , and its closure in the wake of the 1893 national economic crisis prompted Kirk to retire away from the city that still bears his name.

"Early on this process, we had thought about ways to sort of honor Indigenous names, and for many very good reasons, we moved away from that," Deputy Mayor Neal Black said during a discussion in September. "And I think once we've moved away from that, this way of honoring the history, the steel mill, it's meaningful to me, and I think it could be meaningful to a lot of longtime Kirklanders."

The runners-up were The Rise District and The Union District, with a last-minute entrant provided by the Kirkland Heritage Society: the Kellett District. It was John George Kellett, another British businessman seeking his fortune in a sparsely-populated Eastside in the late 19th Century, that decided to name a fledgling town after Kirk. Among other reasons, that name was discarded as being potentially tricky for newcomers to spell.

Though Kirkland is clearly taking the idea of a marketing campaign as a way to raise the area's profile seriously, the future of the neighborhood will almost certainly hinge more on economics. Earlier this year, the Kirkland Council gave the 85th Station area zoning code another tweak intended to spur development, extending a "pioneer provision" that gives the first developers prepared to break ground a discount on affordable housing requirements through 2030.

Those tweaks also included added flexibility when it comes to future development agreements, potentially setting the stage for larger buildings than might otherwise be allowed under code today. Also included were prohibitions on townhome development throughout most of the area, a move intended to prevent the area from getting locked in to an underbuilt form.

The Council also took the step earlier this year of fully removing requirements for off-street parking within the entire station area, going further than a new state mandate in the hopes of providing maximum flexibility for potential builders.
But if the area is primed for a future boom, it hasn't arrived yet.

"We know that these areas are well-suited to accommodate future population and employment growth, and they also represent priority areas for transportation funding, so with that in mind we've recently done a lot of work to update the zoning in the station area to support the transportation investments," Kirkland Senior Planner LeAndra Baker-Lewis told the city's planning commission this past spring. "But we haven't seen a notable amount of development that would help bolster those investments."

Though the 85th station area isn't currently the most accommodating place to get around by walking or biking, Kirkland has been endeavoring to make inroads on that front as well. Just this fall, the City opened a new multiuse path connecting Downtown Kirkland and the future bus station. However, that project comes after Kirkland spent $3.7 million to add a third vehicle lane to NE 85th Street around 120th Avenue NE.

Though construction is well underway on Sound Transit's $2.4 billion Stride BRT program, which will include three total lines from Burien to Lynnwood, interest from developers when it comes to creating transit-oriented development near those future stations has been tepid at best.

In Renton, a recent rezone has primed the area around a Stride station that will include connections to two separate RapidRide lines, but builders are not yet beating down Renton's door to get their projects permitted there – a fact that stands in contrast with development activity around the 2 Line in Bellevue .
But there's a chance new Eastside residents would rather live in The Forge than in a neighborhood called Wilburton.

"Once one of these names is chosen, it would be interesting to talk about signage," Kirkland Councilmember John Tymczyszyn said last month. "Being called the Forge District would be a lot more interesting, in my opinion, if there was 100-foot-high steel sign when you drive up 85th and into this district, so that the name kind of resonates with people that visit that area."

articles.title: ‘Portuguese-style’ joins the fray as Port of Peri Peri Chicken prepares for the great Central Seattle chicken war of 2027
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: (Image: Port of Peri Peri Chicken Kirkland)
The walk down 12th Ave can open up access to a wealth of food and drink alternatives beyond the Capitol Hill core.
A few like L’Oursin at 14th and Jefferson have stood the test of time .
Two new projects are taking shape in a recent mixed use building on a block of 12th Ave that saw a skirmish over small business displacement play out during the project’s development.
Paperwork shows the new restaurants taking shape together on the street level of the Tapestry apartments building at 12th and Fir.
One space is being prepared for Cheng’s Dumplings and Noodle , a Taiwanese concept from first-time Seattle restaurateurs Ya-Tzu Cheng and Yu-Fen Liu.

The other will be home to an expansion of Port of Peri Peri Chicken , a fast-casual restaurant chain specializing in Portuguese-style flame-grilled chicken seasoned with African bird’s eye chilis. The franchise chain already has locations in Kirkland and Bothell among nearly 30 outlets in 11 states nationwide.
The arrival of Port of Peri Peri will add to what has become a comically intense wave of new chicken openings across the Capitol Hill area.

High profile investments include the arrival of the San Francisco-born Starbird Chicken chain on E Pike in a portion of the block’s emptied Amazon grocery store and Char the Chicken , the launch of a new grilled poultry concep t from the backers of the scuttled Mt. Joy chicken sandwich chain and a popular food influencer.

Meanwhile, the recent food and drink history on 12th Ave where Cheng’s and the new Port of Peri Peri are being planned includes the unsuccessful fight for Saba Ethiopian to keep its space after it lost its lease on the block amid plans for demolition to make way for the development six years ago.

articles.title: Seattle Center Diwali celebration pushes through disruption by far-right influencers
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Mayor Wilson and the first kid celebrated Diwali (Image: Mayor Katie Wilson)
Community members and families celebrating Diwali at the Seattle Center Armory on Saturday pushed through an attempt by activists to disrupt the festivities.

The confrontation occurred during youth cultural performances at the annual Diwali: Lights of India festival. Attendees stepped in to eject the disruptors — a couple far-right political activists and internet personalities who frequently stage confrontations at public demonstrations and cultural gatherings and some hangers-on — before the situation could escalate further, ensuring the free, all-day celebration continued as scheduled.

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay condemned the hostility and commended the resilience of the gathering. “Diwali celebrates the triumph of light over darkness,” Zahilay said in a statement. “Those who came to spread fear will not define this holiday, and they will not define King County.”
In the wake of the confrontation, Seattle Center and festival organizers underscored ongoing security and safety coordination across the Festál cultural series.

Saturday’s disruption came amid escalated concern and tightened security at Seattle Center, elements the group behind the disruption were surely aware of. The campus was the scene of a deadly shootout this summer during the Bite of Seattle event.
There were no announced arrests in Saturday’s incident.

The Coalition of Hindus of North America called on authorities to confront bias targeting the community. In its statement, CoHNA stressed protecting cultural gatherings. “Unfortunately the response from authorities has been slow or lacking, with a reluctance to even name or call out the anti-Hindu bigotry driving many of these actions,” the organization said.
Presented by nonprofit Northwest SHARE as part of the Seattle Center Festál series, the festival filled the hall with classical dance and music.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson , who attended the festivities with her child, denounced the stunt and effort to cause chaos at the festival. “We condemn the hateful nonsense from bigots who interrupted a beautiful Diwali ceremony at Seattle Center,” the mayor said in a statement.

articles.title: ‘That’s why you go out’ — L’Oursin marks a decade as an island of food and drink independence at 14th and Jefferson
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: L’Oursin, the little French seafood spot at 14th and Jefferson in the intertidal zone between Capitol Hill and the Central District, turns 10 this November. Its owners are celebrating the same way they’ve run the place from day one — their way.
A decade, a pandemic, and one bar next door later, they’re still at it, and still clearly having fun.
“There were just so many unknowns for us,” said co-owner and bar manager Zac Overman . “We’d never done this before. We were kind of rolling the dice on this neighborhood.”

L’Oursin opened in November 2016 after eight years of planning and a community fundraiser backed by 183 supporters. In 2023, Overman and chef and co-owner JJ Proville added Bar Bayonne next door. Together, they make up a small independent island in a dining scene increasingly dominated by multi-location restaurant groups.
“We’re craftspeople,” Proville said. Running a business on top of cooking and bartending is the hard part. “If you’re going to be around for 10 years or 15 years, you need to pace yourself.”

Some of their best moments weren’t planned. On opening night a decade ago, nobody had stocked empty bottles for juices behind the bar, so L’Oursin’s wine director ran home to grab some. One carried the label of a small Olympic Peninsula wine producer. A friend of the producer happened to be dining that night, spotted it, and made an introduction that eventually led to a liqueur collaboration now several years on the market.
“It’s how small this town is,” Overman said, “and how little things weave themselves together.”
When L’Oursin opened, E Jefferson looked ready to take off with multiple food and drink ventures from an eclectic mix of owners.
“It didn’t exactly happen,” Overman said.

Still, there are bright spots: Peloton is going strong with its own 10-year anniversary marked earlier this year, a vintage shop and coffee shop recently opened nearby, and a five-over-two development is planned next door replacing the building where one of the neighborhood restaurants failed.
“The more there is, the better off the neighborhood is,” Overman said.
It’s a short walk from the heart of Capitol Hill, Proville points out, and you can actually park.
Staying independent, Overman said, is largely about quality of life. “I couldn’t imagine driving across town to check in on another business and seeing how that’s being managed.”
The owners still do the unglamorous work, too. Just recently, Proville said, the two were stocking toilet paper together. “We’re still kind of a mom and pop shop.”

L’Oursin has grown from within, promoting line cooks to chefs along the way. “I’d love to have more money to play around with,” Overman said. “But I do love that it’s still kind of scrappy and bootstrappy.”
Bar Bayonne grew out of the pandemic, when L’Oursin kept the lights on as a market. Long after dining rooms reopened, people kept stopping by during the day looking for wine and sandwiches.
The vacant space next door was the answer: a daytime spot in a neighborhood short on lunch options, and a new home for the wine shop that had been squeezed into L’Oursin’s dining room.
The two share bread, a walk-in, spirits, and cross-trained staff, but run separate wine programs, with Bayonne’s shop leaning toward affordable weeknight bottles.
“The edges are blurry in a really friendly way,” Overman said.
L’Oursin once ran a tasting menu alongside its à la carte offerings, something Overman now calls insane. After the pandemic, diners wanted comfort.

“We can’t go back from a smash burger fried chicken pop-up into a tasting menu again,” Overman said. “Let’s meet in the middle somewhere.” Today, the menu is a hybrid: steak frites, but still exciting seafood.
Costs have climbed in sneaky ways. The recycling bill alone went from about $500 to $800 a month. “People don’t talk about the utilities,” Proville said.

The steaks now use local Washington beef instead of 21-day dry-aged cuts, but Proville still shops Uwajimaya for less-loved fish like yellow-eye rockfish collars, and the restaurant buys from 20 to 30 vendors, including farmers and foragers.

The owners figure business splits about 50-50 between regulars, some coming in for all 10 years, and destination diners. The Monday burger, $16 with fries, is designed to bring people to the bar. “Don’t be intimidated,” Proville said.
Proville’s advice for anyone opening a place: skip the brand new build-out and find a space with infrastructure already in place, the way Bar Bayonne inherited a working bar.
Overman’s tip for neighborhood diners: Watch the pop-ups, where some of the most exciting food in town is happening.
For anniversary week, the owners plan to bring back a few favorite dishes from the first decade. Overman’s pitch to the neighbors around E Jefferson? Come sit at the bar.
“Meat and potatoes,” Proville said. “That’s French food.”
With a lot of butter. “That’s why you go out,” he said.
L’Oursin and Bar Bayonne are located at 1315 E Jefferson. Learn more at loursinseattle.com .

articles.title: With the return of Midnight Movies, group announces ‘soft opening’ for new operator at Capitol Hill’s Egyptian Theatre
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Recent WFLM programming included a screening of the original Halloween (Image: @d_j_notsogood )
“Midnight Movies” are returning to Capitol Hill as the WFLM Seattle collective says it has been given the go ahead to begin its “soft opening” operating the historic Egyptian Theatre .
The group is getting a jumpstart on formal announcements of the new era for the old theater with a full schedule of upcoming midnight screenings. “Ten bucks,” the flyer promises.
Things kicked off over the weekend with a showing of cult classic 90s adventure flick Hard Ticket to Hawaii — “bad acting, unnecessary nudity, and a mediocre plot,” one succinct summary reads.

In September, WFLM and the E Pine theater building’s owner Seattle Central told CHS they are working out details of a long-term lease for the venue that has been available for events but hasn’t been serving the public regularly since a major water pipe break damaged the landmark former Masonic Temple in November 2024.

WFLM has been part of this year’s pop-ups in the Egyptian as Seattle Central opened a schedule of one-time showings and special screenings to light the theater back up after a long closure following the water pipe break and the exit of SIFF .
The school ha\s been looking for a new long-term tenant for the theater that has been showcasing arthouse, classic, and international cinema since 1980.

The group says it plans to operate the Egyptian similarly to Santa Ana’s Frida Cinema with programming centering on repertory cinema, crowd favorites, forgotten titles, and the return of late-night midnight movie screenings.

articles.title: Search begins for new leader for downsized King County Regional Homelessness Authority
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Already on the shakiest of ground as Seattle and surrounding cities pull back funding plans, the King County Regional Homelessness Authority needs a new leader to oversee its downsized future.

The authority has announced CEO Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation. Hired in 2024 as the authority’s fifth leader, in the KCRHA announcement, Kinnison said that she was brought on to “assess and rebuild a young organization that had significant challenges,” citing pride in “surfacing structural issues in our finance department.”
Her resignation, the announcement reads, follows a “forensic evaluation that identified historical deficiencies in the agency’s internal controls and financial systems.”

CHS reported here on the details of the deficiencies as the authority’s shortfalls built over years to a $16.7 million hole . Under shifting priorities and funding and tied up in bureaucracy and process, service providers spent far less grant money than budgeted, which cut the administrative fees KCRHA was set to earn.

KCRHA also spent $3.3 million beyond its funding caps on Salesforce, temporary staff, and legal fees, and racked up $2.4 million in interest by running overdraft balances in the King County Investment Pool, a county treasury structure that manages operating funds and provides liquidity for regional public agencies.
In 2027, KCRHA will transfer local contract administration back to Seattle and King County, refocusing the agency on a smaller portfolio of state and federal responsibilities.
The downsizing of the authority began this summer as officials were forced to restructure the KCRHA after the audit was revealed.
The KCHRA’s budget was proposed as $205 million in 2026 with about 60% coming from Seattle and the rest from the county and state and federal pass-through grants.
According to the announcement, Kinnison offered her resignation in recognition of these pending changes to the agency’s mission and scope.

Governing Board co-chair County Executive Girmay Zahilay thanked Kinnison for leading regional coordination “amid a shifting federal landscape and structural issues within the authority” while Mayor Katie Wilson focused on her office’s responsibility to Seattle residents to address financial challenges. The leaders say they plan to recommend interim leadership to the board soon.
Others are calling for the plug to be pulled. King County Councilmember Rod Dembowski and Seattle City Councilmember Maritza Rivera have made repeated calls for the authority’s full dissolution.

The authority was formed as officials pledged the new effort would consolidate efforts to address the homelessness crisis at a broader, more regional level. At one point growing to a $250 million a year effort, KCRHA was officially established in late 2019 through an Interlocal Agreement between the county and the City of Seattle under then- Mayor Jenny Durkan and then- King County Executive Dow Constantine .

articles.title: Surfeit Rock
articles.author: Dave Segal
paras: The inaugural Baba Obscura festival took over a hot zone in Pioneer Square November 5–8, and if you had the energy and alertness, you could’ve crammed a month’s worth of compelling music into four nights. With Freakout Fest on hiatus, Baba Obscura had big shoes to fill, and it did so admirably. There were some minor hitches and late start times, and the sets at Baba Yaga seemed to draw far larger crowds than those at AXIS and Central Saloon, but overall things seemed to run smoothly. Here are some highlights that I experienced. Your mileage will surely vary.

FROND Seattle quartet Frond were in progress when I entered Baba Yaga, and their Cocteau Twins-lite shoegaze songs were spectral and woozy, with vocalist Jewel Loree—who also plays in the Grizzled Mighty and Golden Idols and hosts KEXP’s Astral Plane show—finessing some nice dubby bass lines. Then a switch seemingly flicked and they launched into high-energy psych-rock, followed by a Wooden Shjips-style motorik jam. What a pleasant surprise. Frond currently have no music online, but you should keep tabs on them.

WEEP WAVE Seattle trio Weep Wave present as blue-collar hard-rockers, but, thankfully, they are so much more than that. Sure, they have their share of melodic anthems that would please fans of Protomartyr or the Hold Steady. But beyond the meaty and torqued guitar and bass riffing in their existential songs about space and death, there be weird electronic elements and club-friendly beats that emanate from a synth off to the side of the stage. Boozy, air-punching rock can merge with EDM (plus some sine waves reminiscent of Kraftwerk ca. Radio-Activity ) and get the ladies—and fellas—moving. And I heard some deceptive funkiness à la Led Zeppelin and Blurt in a couple of songs, while another possessed the fierce vibes of Killing Joke’s “Wardance.” Interesting rock is not a plentiful commodity in 2026, but Weep Wave deliver a potent metallic KO onstage. Look out for them.

JJUUJJUU Led by Desert Daze boss Phil Pirrone (who’s also one of the folks responsible for starting Baba Obscura), JJUUJJUU unabashedly reveled in free-flowing psychedelia from the get-go. The pick-up band included cowboy-hatted Night Beats guitarist Danny “Lee Blackwell” Rajan, who served as the wild card, generating wild guitar eruptions amid the three long improvisations. Combining grandiloquent stoner-rock with instrumental sprawl à la the Doors’ “The End” and Perrone’s occasional old-school, longhair-rock howl, JJUUJJUU revived the spirit of the on-hiatus Freakout Fest. They also had a very cool motorik cruiser, which would become the motif among the groups I saw at BO.

SPOON BENDERS Portland trio Spoon Benders’ churning frenzy of garage-rock, psych-rock, and punk triggered a mosh pit that became increasingly large and violent throughout their Baba Yaga set. It felt like the floor was buckling—maybe because one of the moshers was a mountainous dude who could’ve been a Seahawks offensive tackle. Bassist Kate Black sang with the angsty gravitas of Thalia Zedek and Jennifer Herrema while drummer Mike Amster flexed rapid-fire fills à la Keith Moon. Guitarist Leo Pastor kept things swerving and bruising—just like the human bumper cars in the pit.

MDOU MOCTAR What a whiplash transition this was. Sans band, Nigerian guitarist Mdou Moctar sat down with his electric guitars and unspooled raw desert-blues virtuosity, peppering that with soulful plaints in his native Tamasheq and shouts of “Go!” The loving crowd clapped along nearly continuously to his sinuous riffs that could’ve spiraled on to infinity with no complaints. He also told a long, charming anecdote about how one can learn more from travel than from reading books. ‘Twas a privilege to witness.

PACKAGING Arriving a bit late to Packaging’s AXIS performance, I encountered them in sluggish ballad/slack shoegaze mode. Eventually, though, they a krautrock banger upon us that displayed them at their aerodynamic best. Damn near everyone’s gotta have a motorik jam these days, which is as it should be. For the last song, Packaging broke out the cowbell and flute, which more rock groups ought to be doing. This abstract intro led into a ferocious krautrock steamroller that aspired to the zenith of Can’s “Mother Sky.” You gotta aim high, y’all.

ROSE CITY BAND Dag, after packing out Tractor Tavern last December, Portland’s Rose City Band played to maybe 40 patrons at AXIS. A travesty for a Friday midnight slot, but that didn’t deter guitarist/singer Ripley Johnson’s bearded, nonchalantly brilliant bros from turning this mother out with an economy of movement that would’ve impressed J.J. Cale . Easygoing, cosmic country rock is RCB’s default setting, and they are the greatest modern practitioners of that art. All of the musicians are masterly, but Barry Walker Jr. on pedal steel really launches RCB to the most exalted plane of the genre. And as their set wore on, I became convinced that Johnson’s guitar tone resides on the godly level of the aforementioned Cale’s, Jerry Garcia’s, and Agitation Free’s Lutz “Lüül” Graf-Ulbrich’s. Did RCB have a motorik joint, too? Of course , silly, and it ruled. At one point, though, RCB shockingly detoured into a shimmering disco/yacht-rock number, replete with the beat from Hall & Oates’ “I Can’t Go for That (No Can Do).” Reader, it worked! Wish you were there.

NATHAN NOTHING Nathan Nothing (aka Nate Quiroga) ain’t your typical synth-wielding electronic musician. No static, furrowed-brow stage demeanor for him. The former Mad Rad MC/producer and Iska Dhaaf leader instead jumps around, dances, and bounds into the crowd to rap and sing in an FX’d chipmunk voice about poverty, punching Nazis, and feeding the poor and eating the rich. With ex-Crypts member Bryce Brown on drums and Night Fortress’s Blair Field on downtuned guitar, Nathan Nothing creates clubby goth music that leaves disco balls in shards. There’s dilapidated house music, brutish, song-based electronic music in the Meat Beat Manifesto vein, and even the odd post-punkish ballad. But mostly, these are dance-in-the-ashes dystopia soundtracks. For makers of such dark music, they emit good, positive energy.

THE SPYRALS I only caught about 15 minutes of LA trio the Spyrals’ set, but their stripped-down, ’60s-rooted garage-psych displayed crafty songwriting and excellent dynamics. A pity I had to exit early to see the Gories, who went on 13 minutes after their designated start time.

THE GORIES “I forgot to tune my guitar, so you’re in for it,” announced Mick Collins before the legendary Detroit garage-rock group’s incendiary performance in Baba Yaga’s absolutely packed basement. (Yes, Collins has moved to Brooklyn, but he’ll always be a Detroiter to the core.) No matter, as Collins and Dan Kroha’s dual, barbed-wire guitar attack cut through bullshit rock excesses with their usual primitive cunning. Along with drummer Peggy O’Neill, the Gories pare rock, soul, and blues (the latter two repped by ace covers of Eddie Holland’s “Leavin’ Here” and John Lee Hooker’s “Boogie Chillen”) to their most vital essences. O’Neill’s kit includes snare, tom, tambourine, and no cymbals. She makes Mo Tucker sound like Neil Peart. It’s not easy to do this without sounding like bloodless museum curators, but the Gories are ultimate real ones in the underground, and have been for four decades. They still got it, and then some.

THE INTELLIGENCE Former Stranger Music Genius Lars Finberg left Seattle for California many years ago, and a lot has changed with his music since then. I’d somehow missed his last few albums, in which he ditches his wry garage-rock subversions for a bizarre electronic-music direction, but with interludes of odd-cadenced crooning and guitarlele (?!) strumming. “What are you laughing at, man? It’s the only guitar I can afford,” Finberg quipped to scattered chuckles. Bedecked in an oversized ballcap and green Converse All Stars at a sparsely attended Central Saloon, Finberg sat behind a Crumar Mojo keyboard and began with some spacey jazz-fusion that explains why he titled his latest album Witches Woo . His was a set of baffling tangents, which one hardly ever sees/hears anymore. A downer, Nilsson-ian ballad segued into a killer bleepy techno cut. A Señor Coconut-esque cha-cha preceded a funky, µ-Ziq-like chiller. During one excellent banger, Finberg shouted, “That sounds like Ten Inch Nails [ sic ]. Give it up for Chris the sound guy!” The Intelligence’s crowd may have been unjustly minuscule, but everyone there went home with a unique memory. Do you know how rare that is?

ZOOKRAUGHT My first Zookraught show—a benefit for orgs helping Palestinians—happened last year under a bridge in an unlovable part of SODO. The DIY/off-the-grid nature of that gig seemed like the Seattle threesome’s ideal habitat. So it was a bit strange to witness them in a conventional club, but they thrived there, too. Zookraught make careening post-punk with serious fuck-or-fight energy. They sweat revolutionary queer youth power. Primal-scream catharsis is their default mode, and they’re artful with it, despite (because?) of all the chaos sparking around them. Zookraught draw you in with their colorful, unusual appearance and keep you riveted—and riotously moshing—with exceptional command of their instruments. They seem destined for much bigger things.

THE BLACK TONES Talented twins Eva and Cedric Walker have added a guitarist, bassist, and keyboardist to the Black Tones, the better to manifest their more expansive new album, Diamond Ruby Night , their first in seven years. Speaking of additions, did Cedric gain more muscle? His drumming sure seemed to indicate so. Anyway, Central Saloon felt way too small for the Black Tones’ arena-ready goth-leaning rock and new wave. The Diamond Ruby Night songs’ subjects are dark (mental health issues, encounters with prison inmates whom Eva’s met, death, etc.), but the music’s uplifting. Right now, I like the early Black Tones incarnation a little better, but the new version is very accomplished and leaves me wondering if opening slots on upcoming tours by U2, the Cure, or Echo & the Bunnymen are out of the question.

THE BLACK ANGELS The music airing over the PA before Austin, Texas psych-rockers the Black Angels took the stage at a clusterfucked Showbox was fantastic, and likely chosen by the band. Songs by Bruce Haack, Pearls Before Swine, the United States of America, Wolfgang Dauner, and the Zombies, among others, proved that they have impeccable taste. I wish that the Black Angels’ music were as interesting as their record collection.

Don’t get me wrong—the Black Angels are fine, and they still have the ability to draw 1,130 punters on a Sunday night. But I’ve never understood the fuss that many have made over them. Despite the majesty of many of their songs, the Black Angels strike me as Psych 101—basic and straitlaced. A slow and sinister tune such as “Black Grease” is cool, but its similarity to Loop’s “Too Real to Feel” reveals how that British group imbue the blueprint with more edge and lysergic potency.

Anyway, the Black Angels are currently celebrating the 20th anniversary of their debut album, Passover , which they pretty faithfully replicated. It’s a remarkably consistent album, verging on the monolithic. The dominant style is menacing, methodical, and rhythmically blocky, with rudimentary rock riffs blown out to massive dimensions through FX and punishing volume; my ears are still ringing, even though I wore quality earplugs. Whoever was working sound had everything dialed in wonderfully, especially Misti Hamrick and Jake Garcia’s basses.

A friend at the show summed up the Black Angels’ tempos with a gesture: moving his hand horizontally across his torso in a straight line. It took till the 11th track, “Bad Vibrations,” for a rave-up to appear. “Push It” featured the only real danceable beats. “Firefly” introduced a rare diversion with a more buoyant and whimsical tone. And I dug the liturgical Spiritualized vibe of the intro to “Call to Arms.”

Folks began to file out of the club in droves around 10:45 p.m. (90 minutes into the set), but if you stayed till the end, you were rewarded with the night’s most exciting cut, the outré freakout—à la Mercury Rev’s “Syringe Mouth,” albeit not as wild—known as “Molly Moves My Generation.”

It’s weird to be the lone dispassionate observer in a sea of devotees; my ears are still ringing from their cheers. But I’m happy for everyone who loves the Black Angels, and the band did brisk business at the merch table.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, November 9–15
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: (MUSIC) For over 40 years in Pussy Galore, Blues Explosion, Boss Hog, and other feral units, ex-Ivy Leaguer Jon Spencer has adopted a lewd, shit-kicking persona, the better to make rock and roll sound savage, gritty, and reckless. It’s a shtick, sure, but Spencer’s utterly riveting with it. Even in his 60s, dude still rages. Late-career garage-rock heaters such as Spencer Sings the Hits! , Sick of Being Sick! , and the new Songs of Personal Loss and Protest prove that Jon can still find countless ways to transform primal urges into sonic art. With drummer Spider Bowman and bassist Kendall Wind in tow, Spencer continues to convert his anger at the state of the world and sadness over personal hardships into adrenaline-spiking, soul-inflating rock. ( Sunset Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL
Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean: Celebrating 30 years of Fugees’ The Score

(MUSIC) Lauryn Hill is one of hip-hop’s truly outstanding rappers. Her name is on two albums in the hip-hop canon—the Fugees’ The Score (1996) and her solo work The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998). There is also the raw boom-bap/dancehall style track “Lost Ones,” which is on Miseducation . It alone put any doubt about her skills on the mic in the grave and solidified her reputation among the elite. And this, ultimately, is what matters in the game or rap and reality: her mic skills, her impeccable record, her undying commitment to what has almost entirely vanished from present-day rhymes; namely, “saying something” and never “fakin’ the funk.” So, let’s just show Hill the respect she deserves; few golden era rappers can match her accomplishments. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 8 pm, all ages ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(MUSIC) When the world is on fire, radical compassion is one weapon, and trauma-bonding through bleak, back-alley art-rap is another. There are only two options. Armand Hammer, the binary star comprising New York rappers billy woods and Elucid, has that medicine, and their latest effort, last year’s acclaimed Mercy , a second team-up with everywhere man The Alchemist, takes the world to task. Politics, social ills, and petty annoyances are all handled with typical street corner soothsayer panache, woods stringing together rap-noir micro vignettes that Elucid bounces right back in the form of raspy, big picture, stream-of-consciousness bars. Never ones for undue optimism, the two emcees have nevertheless hit middle age with a head full of steam, itself a testament to the ability to thrive in the face of the static we’re all forced to wade through daily. AH continues to be a crucial antidote for the common ill, and only seems to be getting better with time. ( Crocodile, 8 pm, all ages ) TODD HAMM

(LITERATURE) Andrew Joseph White’s 2022 dystopian fantasy horror young adult novel Hell Followed With Us established him as an author to watch and attracted the notice of The Matrix director Lilly Wachowski, who is currently co-producing an anime-inspired film adaptation. His first book for adults, 2025’s You Weren’t Meant to Be Human , is a gruesome, transgressive trans body horror tale set in Appalachia. White incorporates his experience as a trans bi man with autism into his books and uses fear to plumb the terrors of our present-day existence. His newest book, You’re No Better , is a young adult psychological thriller about Morgan, a 17-year-old autistic trans boy who testified against his own serial killer father, putting him behind bars. He must prove to a predatory true crime documentary crew and his own mother that he is nothing like his dad. Given the relentless demonization of trans teens in the news lately, this novel’s message couldn’t be more timely or urgent. ( Third Place Books Lake Forest Park, 7 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(FOOD) Show up to Ravenna Brewing on Thursday to slurp four soups whipped up by four local breweries and restaurants all vying to be the winner of the coveted Golden Ladle. It is Ravenna’s fifth annual Battle of the Soups. This year the competition includes Hopvine Pub, Watershed Pub, Layers, and Big Time Brewery. All benefits go to Washington Wild. All soup goes into your belly. What soups will they be? It’s a secret. Tickets cost $25 and get you a 5 ounce serving of each soup. ( Ravenna Brewing, 5–7 pm ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(PERFORMANCE) Alex Tatarsky, who once made headlines by pulling a hoax at the Andy Kaufman Awards in 2013, where they announced they were Andy’s daughter and that he was still alive, says their absurdist performances live in “the uncomfortable in-between zone of comedy, dance-theater, performance art, and deluded rant—sometimes with songs.” Their solo show Sad Boys in Harpy Land was commissioned by and premiered at Abrons Arts Center in 2023 before transferring Off-Broadway to Playwrights Horizons later that year and comes to On the Boards November 12–14. In their “magnum o-pussy,” Tatarsky reanimates tortured characters from sources ranging from Seinfeld to Goethe and collages them into a bildungsroman about “a young Jewish woman who thinks she is a small German boy who thinks he is a tree.” Experimental electronic musician Shane Riley, director Iris McCloughan, set designer Andreea Mincic, and lighting designer Masha Tsimring also contribute to the “tour de farce.” It’s not for the faint of heart—be prepared for chewed-up sardines and mandatory audience participation—but you may walk away feeling a little less alone in our current dystopian nightmare. Read the full interview with Alex from our November issue . ( On the Boards, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL
Radio Gaza & Wo’Pop Present: A Benefit For Palestine

(MUSIC/FUNDRAISER) If you’ve been feeling helpless on your doomscroll, here is something positive for you to actually do! Radio Gaza is a series that uplifts and celebrates Palestinian culture through music, art, poetry, and fundraising. Their next event is at Clock-Out Lounge and will benefit the organization Heal Palestine. The night is co-presented by KEXP’s Wo’Pop, and the lineup includes musicians Clarissa Bitar, Shelby Natasha, Intisaar (who was just featured on The Stranger ’s live music podcast, Noise Complaint ), PEN, and KEXP DJ Jyoti B.Fly. There will also be henna tattoos by Jo Sleem, poetry and Tatreez art by Hala Saleh, merch by Sweetmalson, and art from Seattle Artists for Palestine. All of this, plus Arabic treats and beverages by Ya Hala. ( Clock-Out Lounge, 8 pm, 21+ ) NICO SWENSON

(LITERATURE) New York-based author Min Jin Lee is best known for her sprawling Korean family epic masterpiece Pachinko , which was a 2017 finalist for the National Book Award for Fiction and spawned a similarly critically acclaimed TV adaptation on Apple TV+ in 2022. Almost a decade after Pachinko , she’s back with her highly anticipated follow-up American Hagwon , which is just as ambitious in its scope. The novel follows the saga of the Koh family, which includes parents John and Helen and their three children—Bo, DH, and Mido. After their peaceful middle-class life in Korea is torn apart, they must leave Seoul for Sydney and then Southern California, where they grapple with a new reality, start over from scratch, and grasp for a better future. “Hagwon” refers to a Korean tutoring center, where students strive for excellence, and the book asks questions about the faith we place in academic institutions and the cost of pursuing success. Like Pachinko , it’s a nuanced critique of the American Dream and a portrait of the Korean diaspora, and the Kohs will root themselves in your memory forever over the 656 pages. ( Meany Hall, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(VISUAL ART) About an hour’s drive north of Seattle, there’s a magical place called Pilchuck Glass School where the world’s top glass artists convene throughout the year to whip miraculous glass art into existence in boiling hot shops and less-hot cold shops. The campus is a work of art in its own right: It spreads out like a 1970s hobbit fantasy complete with forests threaded with secret paths, stained-glass follies, and treehouses where acolytes retire to revel at the end of a long day’s work. The school isn’t typically accessible to the public, which makes the annual Light the Forest even more special. The event—a self-guided walking tour—unfolds on two dusky November nights, during which the already-ensorcelling Pilchuck campus transforms into an immersive light installation ablaze with neon. This year’s artists are Seattle-based glass baddies MiNHi England and John Sharvin (who both appeared on season 3 of Blown Away ). Did I mention it’s magical? I can’t overemphasize how utterly enchanted it is. This year, they’re also offering day-of workshops, so you can walk away with your very own neon creation or hand-blown ornaments. ( Pilchuck Glass School ) AMANDA MANITACH

articles.title: Slog AM: Oregon Man Rescued from Bucket List Sailing Trip, Seattle Officials Support Macklemore, Nvidia CEO Had Affair with Chinese Spy
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Proud Boys disrupt Diwali celebration: On Saturday, far-right influencer Jake Lang, a pardoned Jan. 6 rioter, and others of his ilk interrupted a Diwali celebration at Seattle Center. They carried racist signs that read ‘Deport All Dot Heads’ and ‘Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians.’ Seattle lawmakers including Rep. Pramilia Jayapal condemned the display.

Capitol Hill Crisis Center’s big price tag: The King County Council approved a $45 million purchase of the old Polyclinic building on Capitol Hill with the intention of turning it into a mental health crisis center. Part of the logic of purchasing this building was its central location and its pre-existing history as a medical facility. Renovations shouldn’t cost too much. The county estimated it would take $17 million in renovations. Now, that cost has more than doubled to $35 million due to higher-than-expected construction costs, inflation, and supply chain issues.

Oregon man and one-eyed dog rescued in Pacific Ocean: Against the advice of his friends and neighbors, Harry Blodgett, an 86-year-old Oregon man, and his one-eyed dog, Sasha, set sail on a 30-foot sailboat from Astoria to American Samoa this fall. After 60 days, he was rescued 460 miles from San Diego. His boat had broken sails. They broke two weeks into his trip. While recovering in a hospital, Blodgett said he plans to attempt the trip again.

Salmon arrive in Longfellow Creek: There are salmon in West Seattle. That’s pretty much the news. Southern Resident Killer Whales appeared in the Puget Sound area this weekend, likely chasing these fish for a quick snack.
It was a wet and windy Saturday: Around 85,000 Seattle City Light customers lost power. It’s back on now .
The weather: It’ll be a routine rainy Seattle day. A bit of bluster, but nothing to write home about.

Another possible suit against I-638: The Seattle Public School Board is considering a resolution to pursue legal action against Washington’s new anti-trans sports law. If approved, the resolution will allow SPS Superintendent Ben Shuldiner and the district’s lawyers to sue over the law’s legality.

Wilson and Zahilay Back the Mack: Last week, Seattle’s biggest celebrity Macklemore revealed the US arenas that banned him from performing his Free Palestine benefit tour. Climate Pledge Arena was on that list. The arena’s ownership didn’t comment on the situation. But Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay did. In a joint statement, they said they support Macklemore’s benefit concert to “help meet the urgent humanitarian needs of Palestinians.”

Stephen Miller’s first day as White House chief of staff: In response to last week’s blue wave and the coming Democratic control of both chambers of Congress, President Donald Trump has made far-right ideologue and longtime adviser Stephen Miller his White House chief of staff . Miller is the architect of Trump’s immigration platform and his deportation push. He has no interest in compromising with Democrats and plans to win back the MAGA base with policies that will energize voters. Surely, they will all be evil.
Will UFC’s Dana White be the press secretary? Trump publicly begged White to take the job. But now he says it was all a joke .

Nvidia CEO’s affair with a Chinese spy: Chipmaker Nvidia is in a world of stock market hurt this morning. Shares fell by 7.5 percent Monday, a day after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy. The company lost more than $300 billion of its valuation. According to a WIRED report, a year ago, Huang hired a crisis PR firm that specializes in public scandals, especially around powerful men and their alleged sexual misconduct.
Is that 3,000 tarantulas in your socks or are you just happy to see me? Oh. It was tarantulas .
