There is little public information available about Alice Huang, the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations , a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.
She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.

articles.title: Advent calendars are a daily delight. Unwrap our top 14 picks for 2026
articles.author: Tobey Grumet Segal
paras: If you’re looking to brighten up every day of the upcoming holiday season, these 13 Advent calendars will bring you sweet joy
Revolve’s beauty advent calendars and 11 more beauty Advent calendars we love
Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things

The run-up to the holidays is always a festive affair. It’s a time packed with parties, friends, family and finding the perfect gifts for all your favorite people. But no matter what holiday you celebrate, be it Christmas, Chanukah or Kwanzaa, an advent calendar is always a fan favorite. And though the ceremony of the Advent calendar is in no way new, the sheer glut of choices we have these days is turbocharged to what was available when I was a kid.

A daily ritual that lets you ease into the festive action, Advent calendars give you the small pleasure of a little surprise, but without all the unwrapping. But with so many options, which one do you buy? From wine, cocktails and jewelry to trinkets, pets and art, here’s a smattering of our favorites to cover everyone on your list.

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mae the labrador, who keeps me safe with her keen nose and piercing stare
articles.author: Laura Chegwidden, as told to Deborah Solomon
paras: Before getting her, I would fall, injure myself and then wake up alone. I’ve trained Mae to be a medical alert dog and she has helped me to embrace life again

It was love at first sight. I met Mae, a black labrador, in 2023 when she was 11 weeks old and she melted my heart completely. I have multiple sclerosis, postural tachycardia syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Since having her, I have been able to start living, horse riding and driving independently again.

At the time I was struggling with the physical and mental symptoms of my illnesses and needed a medical alert dog but there was a long waiting list. So I decided to train my own dog with the help of the Medical Detection Dogs charity.

articles.title: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’
articles.author: Maya Yang
paras: Company says schools should control student AI use, but if they block its AI tools, they’ll lose access to search engine
Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search.

Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.

articles.title: Black girls in LA keep seeing women around them getting killed. They’re driving change
articles.author: Abené Clayton in Los Angeles with photographs by Julien James
paras: Black women and girls represent an outsized share of LA homicide victims – frustrated with police and legislators’ failures, they’re stepping up and speaking out to stop the violence

As a child, Tioni Theus was a ball of energy. After school she liked to play golf and dance. On weekends, she’d go to the movies and the mall with her older cousin. Driving back home at the end of the day to her family’s apartment in South Los Angeles, California, she’d ask: “What are we doing next?”

Everything changed when Tioni was 13. Her mother was hit by a car and critically injured, leaving her unable to take care of her daughter. While her mom recovered, Tioni lived with other family members. But the accident left Tioni angry, her older cousin Nafeesah Kincy said, and she struggled to understand that her life had permanently changed.

articles.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
articles.author:
<name>Robert A. Strong, Senior Fellow, Miller Center, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-a-strong-222390"/>
paras: There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens.
The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration.
It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U.S. has seen only two times in the past half-century.
One was the Newt Gingrich “revolution” in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.
The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals.
In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected.

The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making Gingrich the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House.
It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency .

The combative Gingrich emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm. Confrontations over spending led to controversial government shutdowns and the first modern threat to default on America’s debt obligations .
Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity to win a second term.

In the run-up to his bid for reelection, Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft welfare reform legislation and new bills dealing with crime and immigration . Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s the United States had a balanced budget .
Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when Gingrich pushed for impeachment following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky.
Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, survived his Senate trial . Ironically, it was Gingrich who resigned after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process.
Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized.
Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal produced a Democratic Party victory.
That victory was not a surprise; the scale of it was.

Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote and brought new members to both chambers who were younger, more liberal and reform-minded .

They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the government more open, more honest and more accountable . New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law.
A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, would be elected president two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed.

The post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials.
These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an imperial president .
The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – but not without creating their own problems .

All the post-Watergate presidents thought the war powers resolution was unconstitutional , objecting to its restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and U.S. military interventions overseas continued to occur . Special prosecutors conducted many investigations , but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results.
Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and lost reelection to Ronald Reagan , who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics.
Over time, many presidents, especially Donald Trump , dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms.
The large and enthusiastic congressional majorities that took power after the 1974 midterms were energetic but produced a political legacy with complicated and controversial results .
What is the country likely to see in the next few months and the next two years?

Will it be chaos, conflict and occasional compromise, like the politics that followed the midterms in 1994? Or will it be earnest and sometimes heavy-handed congressional efforts to investigate and prevent presidential wrongdoing, like those that swept through Washington after 1974?
Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.
A number of my links to outside sources are links to the Miller Center website. I am currently a senior fellow at the Miller Center.

articles.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
articles.author:
<name>Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-wolf-2768776"/>
paras: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States ; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages , which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease.

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test , by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.
But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.
As a physician who studies early cancer detection , and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group , I have been following this test’s development with interest.

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.

On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test.

But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.
Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.

Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests . These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.

The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.

Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result.

The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers , including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S , such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer.

Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.
In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range .

This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV , which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens , meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.

For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.

The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients . Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body.
Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings.

For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases . Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.

In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening , meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages , so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result.

Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so . In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this.

There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.
Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.
The FDA advisory panel took three votes . While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.

First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.

These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure , but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.

Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test.

This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer.

Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low?

While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.
The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.

If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.

First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a separate coverage determination process , and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is currently US$949 .

It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.

What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with currently recommended cancer screening tests for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.

Andrew Wolf serves as Chair of the American Cancer Society's Guideline Development Group. This is a volunteer position. Opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
articles.author:
<name>Joel E. Correia, Associate Professor in Human Dimensions of Natural Resources, Colorado State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/joel-e-correia-606706"/>
paras: It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money . In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes.

The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development . Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs.

As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political , economic and environment development , we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability.

Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers , an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices.

As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America ,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers , particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision.
But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem.

The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds.
That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure.

In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions.

The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028.
Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings .
Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay.

Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions.

Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term.

Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding , which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings , an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025.
Peña has denied any wrongdoing , while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision.

The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds , including $355 million from the country’s social security system , IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio.

Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest.
Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest.

Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy.

Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration , an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets.

But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules .

Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed , with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending .

Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000 , is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system , producing outages at several banking institutions.

Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings froze simultaneously . Young Ueno employees burned their company cards outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages.
Riot police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped.

This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks.

In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president.

Marco Castillo Ph.D., Paraguayan sociologist, recent graduate and former director of research at the Center for Latin American, Latino and Caribbean Studies at Graduate Center CUNY, and Sheyla Rios Galeano, a Ph.D. Student in human dimensions of natural resources, Colorado State University, contributed to this article.

Joel E. Correia does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: 5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’
articles.author:
<name>Shannon Gibson, Professor (Teaching) of Environmental Studies, Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shannon-gibson-1388776"/>
paras: Nearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem . It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat .

In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher . Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels , and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises .

There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader.

As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks.

As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31 , in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change:
“We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations.

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding . They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target.

Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030.
In reality, affordability is really about priorities.

For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy.

Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels.
The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it.
Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided.

This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “ stabilization wedge ” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy.
Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue.

Scientists, including one of the original authors , have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP .
Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks.
Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding.

At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement.

However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead . Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most.

The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out.
Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding.

In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade . Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting , with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid.

The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster.

Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage . Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside ” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork.
Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel.

At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach.
In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out.

After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened.
At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice.

Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions , where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers.
My team will be tracking what happens , whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.”
Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article.

articles.title: How protection of public land shapes political strategies in the American West
articles.author:
<name>Erika Allen Wolters, Associate Professor of Political Science, Oregon State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/erika-allen-wolters-2350681"/>
paras: Public lands are intricately woven into the fabric of America. Years of data confirms that a majority of Americans, regardless of their political beliefs, want public lands to remain in federal hands – though not everyone agrees on how exactly those lands should be managed. And while it’s not clear that public lands were a crucial factor in the 2026 midterm election results, survey data suggests that it is an important issue in deciding whom to vote for .

Federal conservation efforts began in the late 1800s , with Yellowstone becoming the first national park in 1872. Today, 640 million acres, nearly 30% of the country’s land area , are administered by the federal government for a wide range of purposes, including conservation, forestry, grazing and energy production. These lands are held in trust by the federal government for the American people.

In our studies of the politics of the American West , where the vast majority of U.S. public lands are located, we are seeing efforts to make voters aware of candidates’ views on land protection and to use grassroots political tactics to influence management decisions.
Protesting government efforts to turn turn public spaces into private property, or to allow development on public land, are key ways people show the value they place on public lands.

In 2017, at the start of Donald Trump’s first term as president, U.S. Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, proposed that the federal government transfer land to individual states . The states, underfunded and understaffed to manage the land themselves, would likely have sold the land to private interests . The response created the #KeepItPublic social media campaign and mobilized conservation groups against the bill. Land Tawney, president of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers, said, “ Once that bill was introduced, the hornet’s nest was kicked .” Chaffetz pulled the bill and left Congress five months later.

And in 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, U.S. Sen. Mike Lee, a Utah Republican, proposed that Congress require the U.S. Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service to sell between 2.2 million to 3.3 million acres of public land in 11 Western states. He said the land sale would help “ address local housing needs .”

But conservation groups and other Western lawmakers, including fellow Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy and Republican U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke, also of Montana, declared the proposal a “ threat to the Montana way of life ” and forced Lee to withdraw the proposal.
There isn’t available evidence to suggest that voters choose members of Congress based solely on their views or action about the management of public lands.

But elected officials often swiftly distance themselves from or outright oppose efforts to modify or eliminate public land protections. That response signals they believe their land protection stances play a role in how the public views them.

For example, Trump administration efforts to reduce Bears Ears National Monument and to swap a parcel in Yosemite National Park with a private developer met with opposition from both parties in Congress .

However, that opposition is not always successful at preventing development or natural resource extraction on public lands. In March and April 2026, both houses of Congress passed a resolution supporting mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in Minnesota, despite public outcry about the potential pollution of a vast wilderness.

In 2026, two new groups emerged to call attention to threats to public lands. Protect Wyoming and PAC for Public Lands in Idaho both formed specifically to compile and publicize elected officials’ public lands voting records , especially when those votes affect people’s rights to hunt, fish and enjoy the outdoors.

These groups may be able to tap into core land protection values broadly shared by many voters across the political spectrum . That could put more direct and consistent pressure on politicians to protect public lands.
The Trump administration has moved to limit people from mobilizing in support of public lands.

For instance, Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025, executive order declaring a “ national energy emergency ” has led the Department of the Interior to accelerate its review of proposals for oil and gas drilling, production and refining, and mining, along with other energy-related natural resource development.

A process that used to take one to two years has been reduced to no more than a month . That provides less time for people to review documents, understand what they say and decide how they feel about the proposals. However, 15 states are now suing the Trump administration , saying that fast-tracking violates federal law and seeking court orders to restore the previous process.

And in January 2026, the White House Council on Environmental Quality revised the rules around public comments on proposed federal land management actions. Government agencies are required under the National Environmental Policy Act to give the public a chance to comment on rule changes. It is the primary way the public can raise objections, question the thoroughness of the options, or to provide other evidence to help inform policy. The council significantly shortened, or in some cases eliminated, the time period during which the public may submit comments – though that decision has also been challenged in court, saying the Administrative Procedure Act requires the original amount of public comment.

How the government handles data center development may shed further light on the political power of public lands. Back in July 2025, Trump issued an executive order seeking to “ utilize federally owned land and resources for the expeditious and orderly development of data centers.”
In fall 2026, media outlets and advocacy groups called attention to efforts to develop data centers on public lands , including at least 17 computing campuses in six states.
Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities. Some politicians have questioned the deals on federal land .

These centers were on the minds of voters in the midterm elections, nowhere more than in the Nevada gubernatorial race, where the Democratic challenger won on a platform to oppose projects on federal land . Voter discontent may not stop the Trump administration from moving forward, but it all but guarantees that data centers on public lands will be an issue in the 2028 general election . The degree to which the opposition gains political momentum could be another indicator of how the American public will act to continue to demand that public lands remain in public hands.

articles.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
articles.author:
<name>Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/barbara-a-trish-950711"/>
paras: Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.
A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat , Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data , 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure , housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use , higher utility bills and environmental degradation , outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.

In contrast to many other issues , concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota , population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote , approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care , given their methodological limitations.
These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance : environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version , a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.
Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers . President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”
Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.

What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform : “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.

articles.title: Trevor Noah on AI
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries , a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast . She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”
Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.
When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.
Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone , noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism , the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.
He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.
Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.
Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:
Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.
In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show , an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer .

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.
Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever .

articles.title: Op-Ed: 'Building Charm' Book Offers Guide to Developing Outstanding Neighborhoods
articles.author: Naama Blonder
paras: The following is an excerpt from Chapter 1 of Building Charm: A Hyper-Practical Guide to Developing Outstanding New Neighborhoods by Naama Blonder and Misha Bereznyak, founders of Smart Density. Drawing on international experience and years of hands-on work, Building Charm presents a proven, practical system for creating genuinely appealing neighborhoods, one developed within real-world development and municipal constraints and applicable across a wide range of densities, from low-rise settings to complex high-density environments. Learn more at smartdensity.com .
Why do even our most thoughtful new neighborhoods lack the charm found in older places?

The departure of Modernist planning from traditional patterns of city building, and the problems it created, have been widely discussed and are now well understood. And while these Modernist planning ideas still dominate in many places, it is generally accepted that we now have a superior set of ideas and practices, and they can deliver neighborhoods of the same quality as our older neighborhoods.

These ideas and practices generally follow what we call the prevailing urbanist model — a widely shared contemporary framework for urban development that prioritizes reduced reliance on cars, walkability and cycling infrastructure, access to public transit, well-defined streets and parks, and often medium to high densities with mixed uses. This model represents what is widely considered best practice among urban planners and designers, and it has shaped many of the more successful new neighborhoods built in recent decades.

But while some new neighborhoods can teach a lot about innovative ideas and the implementation of best practices, when it comes to matching the experience that many old neighborhoods provide so successfully, they have surprisingly little to offer.

It took us time to recognize that the prevailing urbanist model itself had fundamental limitations. Both of us had grown up and practiced in places still shaped by Modernist planning, where any improvement felt significant. At that time, relatively few neighborhoods had been built according to the principles of the prevailing urbanist model, making it easy to attribute any shortcomings to implementation issues or local conditions rather than to flaws in the model itself.

However, the shortcomings of the neighborhoods and the principles that produced them became apparent over time: at first, as the novelty of such neighborhoods wore off, and even more so later, after our own attempts to implement the principles of the prevailing urbanist model met with little success in achieving the qualities of traditional cities.
We had a few opportunities to work on projects that appeared to have great potential, but with the design tools we were using, those projects yielded only mundane results.

In a project in the Greater Toronto Area, we were retained to create a vision to transform a 100-hectare area of low-intensity commercial and logistic uses near a train station into a dense, mixed-use community. We worked within a new street network that had already been planned, but we otherwise had a significant level of freedom in the design. We applied the leading principles of the prevailing urbanist model, and also identified a unique opportunity to create a continuous secondary network of mid-block connections that enriched the experience and the opportunities in the neighborhood. However, even at the level of a vision plan, it became clear that the constraints imposed by the pre-established street network would not allow us to achieve our aim.

Another project, in Southeast Asia, initially appeared promising. This project had a spectacular setting, with an existing network of irrigation and flood control canals. Other development projects in the area ignored the opportunity they presented, and usually filled most of the canals. We decided early to take a different approach and integrate the canals in the design, which created an attractive quality. Despite this strong start, as the design developed, it became increasingly clear that its overall character would end up typical of new development in the area, especially in the street experience, which is a critical factor in shaping the feel of a neighborhood. This was disappointing — not because the design wasn’t unique, but because, even with the integration of the canals, we still couldn’t achieve the character and qualities found in older neighborhoods with canals or even in more ordinary older neighborhoods in the same region. While in the previous project we’d been limited by a pre-existing framework, here we were limited mainly by our own ideas.

The failures that we experienced directly and, more importantly, the disappointment we felt when visiting neighborhoods designed by the brightest designers in the field convinced us that we were all still doing something wrong.

articles.title: JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Firmly , a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil , Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect , a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.
Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.
The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.
Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent , an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.
Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.
The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan , a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.
